💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Sam Varley | 19 Nov 2026 23:09.
  • Bradford City and Doncaster Rovers will square off on Saturday in a Yorkshire derby with importance at both ends of the League One table.
  • The hosts sit a point outside of the playoff places following a defeat last time out while their visitors have dropped into the bottom four due to consecutive losses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Sam Varley | 19 Nov 2026 23:09.

Bradford City and Doncaster Rovers will square off on Saturday in a Yorkshire derby with importance at both ends of the League One table.

The hosts sit a point outside of the playoff places following a defeat last time out while their visitors have dropped into the bottom four due to consecutive losses.

Bradford City head into their first League One game of November at the weekend following an international break with the hopes of returning to winning ways and moving back into the top six.

After winning promotion from League Two and losing in the League One playoffs in the last two seasons, the Bantams picked up where they left off in early 2026-27, winning five of their first seven outings before Graham Alexander departed for Preston North End.

They then turned to Michael Duff and have struggled to continue their hot start since, winning one, drawing four and losing one of their last six league matches with the only victory coming against Stevenage in mid-October.

That did form part of a run of four straight clean sheets for the Bantams, who top the division with nine and have conceded a league-low tally of eight goals, but that came to an end in their last league outing against fellow promotion-chasers and Yorkshire rivals Huddersfield Town, who dished out a 3-0 beating at Mbanq Valley Parade.

Now, at least, on the back of a pair of confidence-boosting cup wins before their break, beating Marine 7-0 in the FA Cup and York City 4-0 in the EFL Trophy, Bradford City now sit eighth, but just two points off fourth spot, and will hope to retake a top-six spot and kickstart another hot streak in League One.

Their visitors, meanwhile, make the trip across Yorkshire in search of a return to winning ways of their own in their battle at the other end of League One.

Doncaster Rovers also won promotion from League Two in 2024-25 and finished 14th last time around on their return to the second tier but now find themselves 21st with just 12 points on the board from 13 games.

That is in no small part down to a poor away record, having lost five of seven games on the road, collected just four points and conceded 16 goals in those.

Two heavy away defeats have come consecutively for Grant McCann's side since a home victory over Sheffield Wednesday, as they lost 3-1 at Luton Town and 6-1 in their last third-tier match away at MK Dons at the end of October.

Having also since played two cup games, beating Rochdale in the EFL Trophy and losing 3-0 away at non-league Kidderminster Harriers in the FA Cup, Doncaster Rovers now head into a tough trip aiming to kickstart an upturn in form in League One and climb out of the bottom four.

Doncaster Rovers League One form:.

Doncaster Rovers form (all competitions):.

Bradford City remain without wide men Josh Neufville and Tyreik Wright, while attacker Bobby Pointon also missed their last outing through injury.

Corey O'Keeffe will continue in a wing-back role in Neufville's absence, while Antoni Sarcevic will start in midfield having served a suspension in the FA Cup for a red card received in their last league game.

George Lapslie, Adam Phillips and Nick Powell will all compete for starts in attack after Jake Beesley led the line with support from Kayden Jackson and Will Swan in the 3-0 defeat to Huddersfield.

Doncaster Rovers continue to contend with several injury issues, as James Collins, Francis Okoronkwo, Matty Pearson, James Husband and Tommy O'Reilly should all remain sidelined.

McCann made some rotations in their two cup games and should make changes from the team that lost 6-1 to MK Dons in their last league outing, with the likes of Robbie Gotts and Will Keane pushing to start after being reduced to substitute appearances.

Hakeeb Adelakun will also challenge for a start on the wing and may join Isaac Hutchinson and Jordan Thomas in support of a lone striker unless captain and key man Owen Bailey returns to an advanced midfield role.

Bradford City possible starting lineup:.

McCracken; Pennington, Baldwin, Pratt; O'Keeffe, Sarcevic, Connolly, Touray; Swan, Beesley, Phillips.

Doncaster Rovers possible starting lineup:.

Simkin; Sterry, Grehan, Byrne, Senior; Broadbent, Gotts; Thomas, Bailey, Adelakun; Keane.

Bradford City have certainly not been at their best in League One since Michael Duff's arrival, but still boasting the league's standout defensive record, and having rebuilt confidence with a pair of dominant cup wins, we back them to come out on top at home to a struggling Doncaster team.

West Ham v Preston Preview: Team News & Lineups as Parker Faces Must-Win Home Debut

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Claretandhugh

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • West Ham United v Preston North End EFL Championship London Stadium Saturday 21 November 2026, 3pm GMT.
  • In a recent development, scott Parker’s first home match as West Ham United head coach is massively important.
  • West Ham have collected one point from Parker’s opening two games and must start closing the gap to the automatic-promotion places.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

West Ham United v Preston North End EFL Championship London Stadium Saturday 21 November 2026, 3pm GMT.

In a recent development, scott Parker’s first home match as West Ham United head coach is massively important. Preston North End are bottom of the Championship and, while Saturday’s fixture is not mathematically must-win, realistically it feels very close to it.

West Ham have collected one point from Parker’s opening two games and must start closing the gap to the automatic-promotion places. After two uninterrupted weeks with much of his squad, this is the first proper opportunity to judge whether the new head coach has begun improving the organisation and intensity of the team.

There is also the troubling matter of West Ham’s home form. I worried before relegation that the vast gaps between the London Stadium crowd and the pitch might turn it into a disadvantage rather than an advantage, and we now desperately need to begin winning there consistently.

The London Stadium has not remotely resembled a fortress this season. Opponents have arrived believing they can frustrate West Ham, exploit the anxiety around the ground and capitalise when the players become nervous.

As one former Championship striker recently observed, visiting teams have been enjoying the London Stadium experience. That situation has to change if West Ham are serious about challenging for automatic promotion.

Recent findings suggest that parker needs his players to begin rapidly and give the crowd something to respond to. The longer this remains goalless, the more Preston will believe their long-ball approach and deep defensive shape can earn them something.

Scott Parker will need to make the London Stadium feel like home.

Industry observers note that west Ham will dominate possession, so the challenge will be using it properly. Passing sideways in front of an organised defence will achieve very little; we need quicker movement, runners beyond the striker and enough tempo to pull Preston out of position.

It has been revealed that I expect West Ham to be considerably tighter defensively following Parker’s first extended spell on the training pitch. However, the international break has not been quite as useful as it initially appeared because several important players were away representing their countries.

Konstantinos Mavropanos was among those absent, while Max Kilman is suspended after reaching the disciplinary threshold at Blackburn. Parker has therefore been unable to work throughout the fortnight with the central-defensive partnership he will need on Saturday.

I suspect Morato will move into his natural centre-back position alongside Mavropanos. That is probably the safe and predictable selection, although I would prefer to see Airidas Golambeckis given the opportunity.

Recent findings suggest that the teenager has generally impressed when called upon and deserves serious consideration. As our examination of Parker’s defensive conundrum against Preston highlighted, the decision appears to be between Morato’s experience and Golambeckis’ encouraging performances.

Recent findings suggest that joël Veltman should start at right-back, while Ezra Mayers deserves to retain his place on the left. Kyle Walker-Peters continues to be assessed, but Parker has two natural and capable full-back options without needing to rush him back.

The biggest selection question surrounds the goalkeeper. I am finding Parker’s team difficult to predict primarily because I do not know whether he will retain Mads Hermansen or turn to Alphonse Areola.

In a recent development, hermansen has produced an inconsistent sequence of performances. He excelled for Denmark against Portugal before making another clanger during the defeat by Norway, which will not have made Parker’s decision any easier.

Sources indicate that there has been considerable pressure for West Ham to make a change in goal, but Areola’s own fitness has reportedly been an glitch. Until Parker confirms otherwise, my best guess is that Hermansen will retain his place.

I suspect Parker will stick with Hermansen.

This is an ideal fixture in which to rebuild the goalkeeper’s confidence, but Preston’s likely use of long balls and set pieces means he must command his penalty area properly. Another nervous display would only intensify the debate but my own choice would be to select Finn Herrick.

I expect Parker to continue with the 4-2-3-1 formation. Arne Engels and Soungoutou Magassa should form the central-midfield partnership, with Divine Mukasa operating further forward.

It has been revealed that magassa gives West Ham a recognised holding midfielder and should help protect a changed defence. That will allow Engels to move the ball forward and support Mukasa rather than both central midfielders occupying similar positions.

Sources indicate that preston’s victory over Southampton was built around an aggressive pressing approach, something Parker will have worked on during the break. I previously argued that West Ham must learn to play through Preston’s press, and this midfield should contain enough composure and energy to do it.

According to recent reports, jarrod Bowen will naturally start on the right, with Edvin Austbø on the left. In my opinion, Austbø has moved ahead of Manor Solomon in the pecking order and deserves a proper run in the team.

Joël Piroe should lead the attack. Parker needs to give West Ham’s most proven Championship goalscorer an extended opportunity rather than continually rotating strikers who have struggled to find any rhythm.

In a recent development, I expect five players who were away on international duty—Hermansen, Mavropanos, Mukasa, Austbø and Piroe—to start. The key defensive change should see Morato move inside to replace the suspended Kilman.

Recent findings suggest that preston earned their first victory under Graham Alexander by beating Southampton before the international break, so they should arrive with renewed confidence. However, both of their Championship wins this season have come at home.

Their away record is dreadful. Preston are winless on the road, having drawn once and lost six of their seven away league matches, including some heavy defeats.

Sources indicate that I expect them to use plenty of long balls, remain compact and try to frustrate West Ham. Even so, the Hammers have far better players and will enjoy the lion’s share of possession.

Sources indicate that quite frankly, it is time they highlighted the difference in quality. If West Ham cannot beat the Championship’s bottom club at home after Parker has been given two weeks to prepare, serious questions will remain about our promotion credentials.

Preston may make the opening stages awkward, but West Ham should eventually have far too much attacking quality. Parker’s team need to play with intensity, move the ball rapidly and turn possession into genuine chances rather than merely dominating the statistics.

I expect a much more organised performance following the international break. Preston’s direct approach may still produce a goal, particularly with West Ham fielding a changed central defence, but this should be the afternoon Parker claims his first victory.

Prediction: West Ham United 4-1 Preston North End.

Industry News: Painful Coventry defeat will send shudder of fear through Newcastle

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newcastle United suffered a painful, chastening defeat, comprehensively beaten by Coventry City in a performance that should send a shudder of fear through Tyneside.
  • It was a dreadful night for the visitors, who conceded four goals for the second successive away game.
  • Newcastle are too easy to create chances against and there is not much that gets you excited when they attack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newcastle United suffered a painful, chastening defeat, comprehensively beaten by Coventry City in a performance that should send a shudder of fear through Tyneside.

It was a dreadful night for the visitors, who conceded four goals for the second successive away game. The manner in which they fell apart was damning. Whatever the supposed style of play, it is not good to watch: long balls are pumped forward for short strikers to chase or compete for in the air against far taller centre-backs. Away from home, it is becoming ineffective.

Newcastle are too easy to create chances against and there is not much that gets you excited when they attack.

Sources indicate that matthias Jaissle’s side did create chances against Coventry, but are not clinical and do not inspire confidence they can be with the players they have. Defensively, they escaped earlier in the season, but are now being exposed and punished. “Not good enough in both boxes,” was Jaissle’s blunt verdict. “To concede eight goals in two away games is not good enough.”.

Recent findings suggest that matthias Jaissle on this evening's defeat at the Coventry Building Society Arena. https://t.co/216NW6Laz8.

Newcastle’s misery was in stark contrast to the joyous celebrations from Coventry. This was a thoroughly deserved first home win of the season for Frank Lampard’s side.

“It was an outstanding performance,” the manager remarked. “We knew we would have to suffer at times against a team like Newcastle. But we were really good at the basics, winning the second balls, winning the duels, those moments are critical. It’s not always about pretty patterns, it’s about work ethic.”.

Industry observers note that the win lifts Coventry level on points with Manchester United and will give them fresh confidence at this level. This could be the start of something special for them.

As for Newcastle, this raises uncomfortable questions about their summer recruitment, with so many expensive players on the bench or playing badly. It also means people will query whether Jaissle’s implementation of “vertical football” is working. The fact Lampard talked so openly about winning the duels to set up the win will anger the German.

According to recent reports, jaissle can point to two bad misses from one of the latest arrivals, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, a £51m buy from Lille, in the first half. But his team are too easy to play through and the defence is an accident waiting to happen.

Even after Sven Botman’s stunning strike offered them a way back into the game, they capitulated at the back as Lewis Hall – who was off colour all evening – and Joelinton’s mistakes gift-wrapped a third for Ellis Simms. A fourth followed for Stephen Mfuni.

In a recent development, ellis Simms off the bench with a big impact! 💥 https://t.co/XynFVxwERV.

You can get a sense of what sort of mode a team are in within the first few passages of play and Newcastle were not sharp or precise. It was sloppy.

That was certainly true of goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who was off his line in no-man’s land trying to snuff out a through ball that he was not going to get. He stood up to deflect it away, but then rashly chased after it, diving at full stretch at the feet of Coventry’s Sidiki Cherif and failing to get the ball. Jack Rudoni coolly sent the Czech goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot.

Newcastle had been awful in their last away game at Leeds, another 4-1 thrashing, and there were many of the same faults on display.

It was not a good first half for Fernandez-Pardo up top. They are mystified in Belgium why he believes he is a centre-forward rather than a winger and he did not do himself any favours here. Newcastle’s best move of the game resulted in Lewis Miley playing in Jacob Murphy down the left. His cutback was perfect for Fernandez-Pardo to sweep home at the near post but instead of trying to make contact, he dummied it, thinking Harvey Barnes was better placed. He was not. It was a baffling piece of centre-forward play.

It had been the easiest 40 minutes Lampard’s side have had since they were promoted, but Newcastle still should have scored before the break.

Nico González spotted the run of Fernandez-Pardo through the middle. He wriggled clear of Bobby Thomas and sat down goalkeeper Carl Rushworth, but the Coventry centre-back got back to block his shot.

Newcastle pressed the self-destruct button early in the second half. A long throw into the box was half cleared. There was a half-hearted attempt to close Cherif down from Yoane Wissa and then a shot that somehow went through a crowd of three Newcastle defenders, including the legs of Botman, and nestled in the bottom corner.

Sidiki Cherif with a STUNNING finish on his first Premier League start! 🤩 https://t.co/EoTB8VCHuR.

It should have been three. Again Wissa was partly to blame, losing the ball in midfield to set Coventry on the counter-attack. When Botman made a mess of a clearance it spun perfectly into the path of Cherif. The net should have bulged but the £20m summer signing from Fenerbahce scuffed wide.

The visitors needed something special to get back into it and it came from the most unlikely of sources as Botman unleashed a rocket from 25 yards.

Sven Botman, that is SENSATIONAL! 🤯 https://t.co/GalkqMs5ZE.

According to recent reports, in a flash the balance of play shifted in Newcastle’s favour. They poured forward in search of the equaliser. Jaissle switched to a 4-4-2 with Will Osula joining Fernandez-Pardo up front, but instead of pulling level, Coventry pulled further ahead.

"We need to improve the things we can control, and right now that's a lot" 🗣️ Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle expresses his disappointment after his side's loss to Coventry 👇 https://t.co/fatJkZYyRM.

According to recent reports, very, very satisfying. It’s so hard to win. We played like the team we want to be here. A team you look at and go there’s so much energy and spirit in the group. We know we are going to have to suffer this season, when we don’t have a lot of the ball. We have to understand it. The level is what it is.

The work ethic, the belief. You get what you deserve. Great finishes. We haven’t quite had the rub of the green this season and that might have helped us nick a couple of more points. I’m a firm believer that you keep going. It was a complete performance. We’ve got to keep our feet on the ground because we’re going to have to do 30+ of those but it’s a great feeling for the players.

[Cherif] is very, very exciting because he is so young. He has got a really good manner. He wants to train, he wants to learn. He’s quite quiet but on the pitch he shows a lot of personality. When you see the quality of the strike and the hold-up play, there’s a lot to come from him.

A win for Newcastle United this evening will take Matthias Jaissle’s side up to fourth in the Premier League and vindicate the members of the club’s hierarchy who insisted they had appointed an elite manager to replace Eddie Howe.

It will also suggest they got their summer rebuild right and everything will point to an exciting future for a newly introduced look team.

Yet, should Newcastle lose against a Coventry City side – newly promoted to the top flight and yet to win at home this season – ripples of discontent will spread through the fanbase and everything about the summer, from managerial appointment to player recruitment will be called into question.

That may seem like an odd thing to write given how wildly different those reactions are but that is where Newcastle find themselves at the moment. We do not actually know if they are any good or what the expectations should be for a young team with a rookie Premier League head coach.

There remains an undercurrent of anxiety among supporters who have seen so many of their best players leave over the last 12 months and be replaced by young, emerging talent from across Europe.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Coventry City and Newcastle United from the Ricoh Arena. Newcastle have played only once there in the league – a 4-1 victory in the Championship back in 2010 when Chris Hughton’s side stormed the league. Their last top-flight visit to the city was way back in 2000, the year Cov’s 34-season spell in the top division ended. Alan Shearer Kevin Gallacher scored at Highfield Road on that occasion, a year after they were sent packing 4-1 by Gordon Strachan’s side by virtue of goals from Carlton Palmer, Paul Williams, Robbie Keane and Mustapha Hadji.

Sources indicate that today’s visit begins with Newcastle in 11th, having bounced back from their Monday night mauling at Elland Road to beat Hull 23 days ago. So bunched is the table, though, that victory tonight would propel them up to fourth. Coventry, by contrast, are 19th after one win and four defeats from their opening five games. If they win they would join Manchester United on six points and leap to 14th, one place ahead of Nottingham Forest, the team they beat last time out before the international break.

In a recent development, frank Lampard’s side responded superbly after being hammered 5-0 by Brighton in their last home game, tightening up in midfield and defence and finding precisely Forest’s weak spots that Oliver Glasner has been unable so far to armour-plate. Taiwo Awoniyi, who was sent off during that defeat by Brighton, is absent serving the second leg of his three-match suspension and Hajii Wright and Aurele Amenda are still some way off returning. Tino Livramento pulled out of the England camp with injury and is likely to be sidelined for a while longer but Matthias Jaissle was more optimistic about his raft of other doubts: William Osula, Lewis Miley, Amar Dedic, club captain Dan Burn, Anthony Elanga and Jacob Ramsey.

Conservation of the tumour microenvironment across organs and species

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 90 min read (17969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~90 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, current understanding of the host tissue response to solid tumours is largely based on investigations of tumour types in isolation1.
  • Solid-organ cancers represent a complex spectrum of pathology, with the intricately associated TME having a pivotal role in disease progression and therapeutic response4,5.
  • Recent findings suggest that previous studies have identified distinct cell subpopulations within the TME based on their gene expression profiles, spatial distributions and functional characteristics17,18,19,20,21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, current understanding of the host tissue response to solid tumours is largely based on investigations of tumour types in isolation1. Given the breadth and diversity of human tumour pathology and contributions of tumour microenvironment (TME) cells to disease progression, pan-cancer analysis is needed to bridge major themes of stromal and immune cell evolution. To date, however, efforts to compare the TME response across cancers have been limited in scope2,3. Here we conduct a comprehensive pan-cancer analysis by algorithmically screening thousands of publicly available single-cell transcriptomic datasets for stromal and immune signatures across species and tissue types. We demonstrate conserved hallmarks of host cell transcriptional programming in response to malignancy across 42 cancer types in more than 2,000 human and mouse tumour samples. These findings are codified as an interactive web atlas (tmeatlas.stanford.edu) and software package (scTME) that will serve as practical resources for the systematic interrogation of the TME in tumours.

Solid-organ cancers represent a complex spectrum of pathology, with the intricately associated TME having a pivotal role in disease progression and therapeutic response4,5. Within the TME, both stromal and immune cells have emerged as key modulators of tumour growth, invasion and metastasis1,6,7,8,9,10. However, different studies (often in single-organ contexts) have shown conflicting roles for these cells in promoting versus suppressing tumour growth11,12,13,14. The heterogeneity of the TME, both within individual tumours and across tumour types, poses a substantial challenge to understanding the functional diversity of tumour-associated stromal and immune cells3,15,16.

Recent findings suggest that previous studies have identified distinct cell subpopulations within the TME based on their gene expression profiles, spatial distributions and functional characteristics17,18,19,20,21. However, these findings stem largely from isolated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies22,23,24, and subsequent pan-cancer efforts have remained limited in size and scope3,25,26,27,28. To our knowledge, the largest cancer-associated fibroblast atlas to date integrates data from 1,116 samples across 10 tumour types29; the largest tumour endothelial cell atlas includes 575 samples across 19 tumour types30; and no specific tumour mural or nerve atlases have been generated. Pan-cancer immune cell atlases have been larger28, especially those focused on individual immune cell lineages31,32,33; however, these typically have not examined immune cell interactions within the broader TME.

It has been revealed that here we integrated single-cell transcriptomic data from 3,381 human and mouse samples across 42 cancer types and 258 datasets to create a definitive TME transcriptional atlas. By mapping this massive cellular landscape, we resolved the stromal and immune ecosystem of solid tumours. Furthermore, by linking enriched subpopulations to poor clinical outcomes, we identified opportunities for future TME-targeted cancer therapies. Key computational predictions are subsequently validated through in vitro and in vivo experiments. Finally, we have consolidated this work into an interactive web atlas (tmeatlas.stanford.edu) and R software package (scTME) that will serve as practical resources for groups investigating the TME.

According to recent reports, to systematically analyse single-cell transcriptomic data, we evaluated every scRNA-seq cancer study published in the public domain between January 2014 and July 2025. Separate queries were evaluated independently for human and mouse datasets within the foundational public repositories for single-cell transcriptomics: the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and ArrayExpress. We screened a total of 3,975 published datasets (Fig. 1a). Studies specific to either blood or central nervous system cancers were excluded from our analysis, as were those failing to meet specific architectural requirements (Methods; see Fig. 1a,b). Our comprehensive screen identified 190 human and 68 mouse datasets (Supplementary Table 1), collectively comprising more than 15.4 million cells. Collectively, these datasets formed the final analytical cohort, comprising 3,381 individual scRNA-seq samples across 42 unique cancer types (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3).

The initial screen examined 3,975 datasets, of which 190 human and 68 mouse scRNA-seq remained after filtering. The combined 258 datasets comprised 3,381 samples and more than 15 million cells. Schematic created in BioRender; Wang, H. https://biorender.com/w8x4pii (2026). CNS, central nervous system. b, Illustration of all cancer types from human (top) and mouse (bottom) included in this study. HNSCC, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma; MPNST, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour; NSCLC, non-small-cell lung cancer; SCLC, small-cell lung cancer. Illustration created in BioRender; Wang, H. https://biorender.com/p0byno1 (2026).

To process the more than 12.8 million human cells from 2,855 samples and 190 datasets (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Fig. 1), nearly an order of magnitude greater than many recent seminal studies3,25,26,27,28,31,32,33,34, we used sketch-based sampling and memory read optimization (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d). We applied three independent approaches for data integration to reduce batch effects: Harmony, scVI and FastMNN (Extended Data Figs. 1e and 2a). We then projected each integrated result onto the full dataset (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Supervised annotation using four methods—canonical marker genes, estimated copy number variation (inferCNV), SingleR and scATOMIC (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 2)—delineated the presence of seven main cell types across nearly all human cancers (Fig. 2a–c, Extended Data Fig. 1e,f and Supplementary Table 4). These encompass principal stromal (fibroblast, endothelial, mural and nerve) and immune (myeloid and lymphoid) lineages, alongside epithelial cells, which were excluded from subsequent characterization to focus on the two core TME compartments. Comparing the three integration approaches (Supplementary Table 5), Harmony demonstrated the most robust integration and was selected for all subsequent evaluations. The three integration approaches also frequently yielded discordant cell-type assignments for individual cells (Extended Data Fig. 2d–f), highlighting the stochasticity and misclassification risks inherent to relying on any single method35,36. To mitigate this, we provisionally pooled all cells assigned to a specific TME lineage by any of the three algorithms (Extended Data Fig. 1g). Misassigned cells within these overlapping pools were subsequently removed through recursive downstream filtering (Extended Data Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 3a–e), generating final, high-fidelity atlases for the six principal TME cell types (Fig. 2d–i and Extended Data Fig. 1i,j).

Abbreviations of cancer names are listed in Supplementary Table 2. d, UMAP embedding of CAFs, manually clustered into four parent populations (outlined and labelled within the UMAP) from a total of seven transcriptionally distinct subpopulations, the latter of which are coloured separately (top left). A dot plot displaying relative gene expression for characteristic markers of the seven transcriptionally distinct CAF subpopulations shown in the left panel (top right). Distributions of CAF subpopulations among tumour samples for different cancer types are also shown (bottom; n = 328,877 cells). e–i, UMAPs (top left), dot plots (top right) and distributions among tumour samples for different cancer types (bottom) for endothelial (e; n = 234,948 cells), mural (f; n = 162,178 cells), nerve (g; n = 7,655 cells), lymphoid (h; n = 1,580,785 cells) and myeloid (i; n = 805,111 cells) cells. Between 3 and 12 subpopulations are identified for each cell type, and one population-defining gene per subpopulation is displayed in the dot plot for each cell type (full list in Supplementary Tables 6 and 7).

In a recent development, we next characterized cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), the predominant stromal population in the TME37. Following our recursive isolation strategy (Extended Data Fig. 1h), we delineated four transcriptionally distinct CAF meta-clusters (Fig. 2d) expressing canonical markers (PDGFRA, LUM and DCN) and lacking non-fibroblast markers (Extended Data Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 4). Specifically, we identified (1) antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs; class II HLA+), (2) immunomodulatory/inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs; cytokine+), (3) myofibroblastic/mechanoresponsive CAFs (mCAFs; extracellular matrix (ECM)+, mechanotransduction+), and (4) steady-state CAFs (ssCAFs; progenitor-like markers+; Fig. 2d), broadly consistent with observations from our previous work38 and that of others25,39,40,41. High-resolution sub-clustering (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Table 6 and 7 and Supplementary Fig. 4) further stratified these into seven subpopulations: two iCAF (CXCL8+ or ISG15+), two mCAF (LRRC15+ or COL4A1+), two ssCAF (PI16+ or CXCL14+) and one apCAF. All seven subpopulations were conserved across nearly all evaluated tumour types and tissues (Fig. 2d, bottom). Of note, apCAFs were nearly universally present, whereas previous studies had found them only in rare tumour subsets6. Furthermore, the human apCAFs that we identified did not express mesothelial markers such as MSLN, which are characteristic of mouse apCAFs42 (Extended Data Fig. 4a).

Industry observers note that comparing relative abundances between tumour and non-malignant tissues (Fig. 3a), both mCAF populations were significantly enriched in tumours (3.5-fold for LRRC15+; 2.7-fold for COL4A1+; Supplementary Table 8), reflecting cancer-induced desmoplasia37,43. Similarly, iCAFs and apCAFs were enriched in tumour samples (6.3-fold for ISG15+ iCAFs, 1.3-fold for CXCL8+ iCAFs and 2.0-fold for apCAFs), consistent with their roles in inducing immune evasion42 or secreting inflammatory cytokines41. Analysing abundance across tumour stage and patient treatment response, we found ISG15+ iCAFs, LRRC15+ mCAFs and COL4A1+ mCAFs significantly enriched in late-stage (III–IV) versus early-stage (I–II) tumours (1.9-fold, 1.3-fold and 1.2-fold, respectively; Fig. 3b). Treatment responsiveness did not significantly correlate with any CAF subpopulation (Fig. 3c). Overall, ISG15+ iCAFs were the most consistently enriched fibroblast subset defining both the malignant state and advanced disease (Fig. 3a–c, blue box).
